The fires became the highest firefighting priority in the US amid widespread drought and ongoing wildfires across the Pacific Northwest in early August. No serious injuries or deaths were reported in Spokane. https://instinctmagazine.com/poland-fore.text: Poland has once again reminded everyone that when it comes to love, the paperwork can be more dramatic than the wedding vows. For many LGBTQ+ couples, saying “I do” in one European Union country still doesn’t guarantee another country will say, “Cool, we’ll file that.” RELATED: Poland’s Top Court Finally Recognizes Same-Sex Marriage—Sort Of Source: Pexels / Photo by freestocks.org Marriage equality in Poland has taken another frustrating detour after the country’s highest constitutional court rejected plans to recognize same-sex marriages legally performed elsewhere in the EU. Apparently, crossing borders is easier than convincing bureaucracy that a wedding is, in fact, still a wedding. Marriage equality meets another legal wall in Poland Just when it looked like Poland might finally start catching up with its European neighbors, the Constitutional Tribunal slammed the brakes. RELATED: Anti-Marriage Equality Campaign Returns to Virginia The court ruled that same-sex marriages performed in other EU member states cannot be entered into Poland’s civil registry, overturning plans that would have brought the country in line with an earlier decision from the Court of Justice of the European Union. It’s the legal equivalent of showing up with a perfectly valid invitation only to have someone insist your name isn’t on the guest list. Source: Pexels / Photo by Monstera Production The unanimous ruling, announced on 28 July, is final and could spark fresh tension between Poland and the European Union over how member states honor cross-border rights. According to the court: plans for the “preparation and issuance of certified copies concerning unions contracted abroad that do not constitute a union between a woman and a man” were “inconsistent with Article 92, Paragraph 1, in conjunction with Article 18 of the Constitution of the Republic of Poland.” The ruling also cited the country’s constitution, which states: “Marriage, being a union of a man and a woman, as well as the family, motherhood and parenthood, shall be placed under the protection and care of the Republic of Poland.” After that, the judges simply… left the group chat. No further explanation accompanied the decision. Donald Tusk was reading a different script The twist is especially surprising because only two months ago, Prime Minister Donald Tusk sounded like he was preparing audiences for a much happier ending. Prime Minister Donald Tusk / Source: donaldtusk His comments followed legal victories tied to a Polish same-sex couple whose 2018 German marriage certificate had long been denied entry into Poland’s civil registry. A November 2025 ruling from the European Court of Justice, followed by a March decision from Poland’s Supreme Administrative Court (NSA), appeared to pave the way toward recognition. Speaking in May, Tusk acknowledged the country’s treatment of same-sex couples in unusually candid terms. “[This is] a matter of human dignity: the right to happiness, the right to equal treatment by the state,” he said. “I would like to apologise to all those who, for many, many years, felt rejected and humiliated. For many years, the state has failed the test.” He also said his government would prioritize complying with the court rulings while making sure any legal changes stayed within Poland’s existing legal framework. Love is complicated. Bureaucracy somehow made it worse. Queer people have always joked that relationships come with enough paperwork already. Apparently, Europe decided to make that joke legally binding. Source: Pexels / Photo by SHOX ART For LGBTQ+ couples, this isn’t just about whether a marriage certificate gets stamped in the right office. Recognition shapes everything from inheritance and healthcare decisions to parental rights and the simple dignity of having your relationship acknowledged by your own country. The latest ruling also creates an awkward political split. On one side is a prime minister publicly apologizing for years of discrimination. On the other is a constitutional court insisting the country’s registry books stay firmly closed to same-sex marriages performed abroad. It’s less “happily ever after” and more “please hold while your rights are being processed.” For now, marriage equality in Poland remains caught between competing visions of the law. And while love may know no borders, the bureaucracy, unfortunately, still seems to have a passport checker standing at the gate. https://en.gmw.cn/2026-08/29/content_389.text: Roundup: China passes healthcare security law, appoints civil affairs minister, ratifies extradition treaty with Hungary Zhao Leji, chairman of the National People's Congress (NPC) Standing Committee, presides over the closing meeting of the 24th session of the 14th NPC Standing Committee at the Great Hall of the People in Beijing, capital of China, Aug. 28, 2026. (Xinhua/Liu Weibing) BEIJING, Aug. 28 (Xinhua) -- Chinese lawmakers on Friday voted to adopt a new healthcare security law, approve the appointment of a new civil affairs minister, and ratify an extradition treaty with Hungary. The votes were taken at a closing meeting of the 24th session of the Standing Committee of the 14th National People's Congress (NPC) in Beijing. Lawmakers also voted to adopt a law on farmland protection and quality improvement, a revised Agriculture Law, a revised National Defense Mobilization Law, and a decision on amending the lawyers law. They also adopted a decision to remove Lu Zhiyuan from the post of minister of civil affairs, and appoint Li Changguan as minister of civil affairs. President Xi Jinping signed five presidential orders to promulgate the laws and the decision, and a sixth one to announce the decision on the personnel change. Zhao Leji, chairman of the NPC Standing Committee, presided over the closing meeting. In the meeting, lawmakers ratified an extradition treaty between China and Hungary. The legislature voted to remove Zhang Youxia as vice chairman of the Central Military Commission (CMC) of the People's Republic of China and Liu Zhenli as a member of the CMC. Lawmakers also voted on several personnel appointments and removals and other personnel-related bills. They also passed a deputy qualification report. While addressing the closing meeting, Zhao said that legislative work should place greater emphasis on safeguarding and promoting social fairness and justice, further improve the socialist legal system with Chinese characteristics, and provide solid legal guarantees for advancing Chinese modernization on all fronts. He stressed the need to strengthen legislation in key, emerging and foreign-related fields, and called for efforts to improve the quality of legislation and ensure that it keeps pace with changing needs. Zhao also chaired a meeting of the Council of Chairpersons of the NPC Standing Committee before the closing meeting, and presided over a lecture for lawmakers afterward. https://www.politico.eu/article/how-to-w.text: STOCKHOLM — Millions of Swedes will vote in a tense general election on Sunday that is set to deliver a new left-wing government or bring far-right ministers into power for the first time. The Social Democrat-led left bloc enjoyed a comfortable lead for months but polls tightened significantly in the final two weeks of the campaign, with one 11th-hour survey suggesting a dead heat . “Two or three weeks ago, we were saying this is a done deal,” said Gustav Karreskog Rehbinder, who is running results forecasts for Sweden’s public broadcaster SVT on election night. “Now it seems that it will be a more exciting night than expected.” Advertisement Advertisement The vote will have potentially significant consequences for security in Europe and the wider debate over integrating the far right into mainstream politics. Here is POLITICO’s guide to the contest, the candidates and the countdown to declaring a winner. How does the election work? There are 349 seats in the Riksdag, Sweden’s parliament, which is located in an imposing waterside building on an island in central Stockholm. The country chooses its lawmakers every four years using a proportional representation voting system, meaning that if a party gets about 20% of the votes across Sweden, it will have about 20% of the seats in the Riksdag. Coalitions are the norm. But there’s a catch: Very small parties are eliminated and get no seats at all if they do not meet the minimum threshold for support of 4% of the national vote. This could be a vital element in a closely fought contest, when the smaller parties may hold the balance of power. Nearly 8 million people are registered to vote and turnout tends to be high — more than 80%. This year, a record number of people are expected to have cast their ballots early, which they’ve been able to do since Aug. 26. If they change their minds, these early voters can vote again on Sunday, canceling their original choices. Regional and local elections take place at the same time. Who gets to govern? After the last contest in 2022, eight parties were elected to parliament and they have been fighting this summer’s campaign in two blocs — one on the left and one on the right. Advertisement Advertisement That means there are only two realistic candidates to be prime minister: the incumbent, conservative Moderate party leader Ulf Kristersson; and Magdalena Andersson, the former PM who leads Sweden’s biggest party, the center-left Social Democrats. Swedish Prime Minister and Moderate Party leader Ulf Kristersson speaks to the media upon arrival to a televised election debate hosted by TV4 in Stockholm, Sweden, on September 10, 2026, three days ahead of the country’s general election. | Jonathan Nackstrand/ AFP via Getty Images Kristersson has run the right-wing coalition for the past four years thanks to influential support from the second biggest party, the far-right Sweden Democrats. They backed him in votes in parliament and drove policy in a hardline direction, including crackdowns on crime and especially immigration. But the Sweden Democrats did not join the coalition cabinet. That could now change. Can the far right enter the government? Kristersson divided opinion in 2022 when he broke a decades-long taboo against working with the far right and did his deal with the Sweden Democrats, who had won 20% of the vote. The SD was founded in the 1980s and some members in those days had roots in neo-Nazi movements. The party has taken steps to clean up its act in recent years, though not to everyone’s satisfaction. Now Kristersson says he will give the SD ministerial seats in government if his side wins on Sunday, as part of an agreement with the far-right leader, Jimmie Åkesson. That would be another huge step for Sweden and one that the opposition has seized on. “Of course this would be a different country with a government with half of the ministers from the Sweden Democrats,” opposition leader Andersson told AP recently. “It would not be good for Sweden if they would get the keys to the ministry of defense or the ministry of foreign affairs.” Kristersson insists he would still be in charge overall. He points to his work with Åkesson over the past four years which he says has revived the economy and cut rates of violent crime and immigration, both of which had been major public concerns. “I can guarantee you that it will only be very skilled and experienced and people with good judgment that would be part of my government,” he told POLITICO. Advertisement Advertisement For his part, Åkesson says it’s time for the SD to take the next step and assume the responsibility of governing. He is eyeing up the chance of becoming prime minister himself at the next vote, due in 2030. The SD sums up its vision for the country with the phrase: “Sweden should be safe, free and Swedish.” What is at stake for Sweden and Europe? Apart from the question of far-right power — which is a political preoccupation across the continent, especially after recent state elections in Germany — both the left and right leaders have traded blows on the question of security, and who will be strongest in standing up to Russia. In a POLITICO interview Andersson demanded that Kristersson come clean after it was claimed that an SD official allegedly promoted pro-Russia narratives and linked up with a Russian state group inside Sweden. For his part, Kristersson in his own POLITICO interview questioned the left bloc’s commitment to NATO , which Sweden has only been a member of for two years. Tim Ross/POLITICO One thing unites both candidates for prime minister: continuing Sweden’s support for Ukraine. In its long history, Sweden has been at war with Russia multiple times and the threat Moscow poses is seared into the national consciousness. Otherwise, the campaign focused on consumer politics — helping ease the cost of living and improve Sweden’s famous welfare state. The two sides made competing promises of a better deal on taxes, housing, health and dental care costs, as well as warnings over the impact of their rivals’ migration policies. When will we know who has won? Swedish broadcasters will release exit poll findings when the voting ends at 8 p.m. local time on Sunday. Advertisement Advertisement Karreskog Rehbinder said he hoped to be able to give an early indication on SVT of how the election will unfold once 10% of the votes have been counted, which he expects to be around 9.15 p.m. If the final tally is extremely close and it’s not clear which side is ahead in the first hours after the voting ends, he said it would likely not be clear until all the counting has finished — which isn’t expected until Wednesday 16 Sept. or later. The Swedish Election Authority usually publishes “an initial provisional allocation of seats” in the Riksdag at around 10.30 p.m. on election night, if enough voting districts have reported their results by then. But even once the final results are known, it will take weeks or perhaps even longer before a new coalition is formed. And if the parliament cannot ultimately agree on a new prime minister, a fresh election could be called. Parties on the right are largely settled in their so-called Tidö alliance — named after the castle where their agreement was signed in 2022. But there have been deeper splits between some of the smaller parties in Andersson’s left bloc, which could prove a challenge to her attempt to stitch together a majority government. “If you look at the prediction markets and polling aggregations, they say exactly the same thing — there’s about a 70% probability of a left-wing win, which is of course much narrower than it was three weeks ago,” said Karreskog Rehbinder, who is the founder and CEO of political tech startup Vera Policy. “That would still be my best guess but it is far from sure.” Advertisement Advertisement

https://www.dailyrecord.co.uk/news/polit.text: John Swinney has failed to say how many jobs will go as a result of his plan to slash the number of health boards across Scotland. The First Minister last week unveiled his ambition to centralise public services - which could see councils forced to merge to save cash - as the SNP Government struggles to plug a £5 billion blackhole in its finances by 2030. Swinney told MSPs that Scotland's 14 regional NHS boards would be reduced to just two covering the mainland - a plan trade unions described as a "slash and burn" approach to reforming the health service. The SNP leader was asked four times during an interview with BBC Scotland today if he could say how roles many would be cut as a result of the proposals. Swinney said: "I can't put a specific figure on that today. I simply wouldn't be giving a comprehensive answer if that was case. "What we've got to work our way through is a programme of reform to make sure we put people right at the very centre of the delivery of public services. "That will apply on all of the public service we take forward. We'll ensure that Scotland is rewired and public services are reimagined." Jackie Baillie, Scottish Labour acting leader, said: "It’s hard to tell whether John Swinney is being evasive or simply has no idea what he is going to do, but either way it’s not good enough. "People’s jobs are on the line and our public services could be plunged into chaos – Scotland deserves to know what lies ahead. "SNP chaos has done enough damage to our services and our finances already. The SNP must come clean about what it is planning, how many jobs are at risk and what it will mean for our public services." Swinney has also signalled his intention to rip up how social care is currently delivered across the country. The SNP Government previously scrapped plans to launch a so-called National Care Service in the face of a backlash from councils and unions. Swinney insisted: "On health and social care, we have to have greater process of integration to make sure the service is seamless, that works in the interests of individuals, and that we can deliver the care that individuals require in their communities. "And that's an open question for us to discuss with not just local authorities, but with trade unions and third sector partners to make sure we use this moment of reform to deliver the best outcomes for the people of Scotland." Put to him that he wanted to see the number of councils to reduce to save money, Swinney responded: "I do, and I want local authorities at a more regional level in Scotland. "We're already having discussions with a number of local authorities who can see the advantages of such an approach. And I want to work with them to take forward such a model. The FM claimed the new "strategic regional authorities" would have "more powers and more responsibilities and greater scope to boost the economy".

https://13wham.com/news/local/warsaw-man.text: Livonia, N.Y. — A Wyoming County man is charged with third-degree rape following an investigation into an alleged sexual assault in Livingston County. David Summers Jr., 21, of Warsaw, allegedly assaulted a 21-year-old woman in Livonia in May, according to the Livingston County Sheriff's Office. The investigation began Aug. 14, and Summers was arrested Tuesday. He was taken to the Livingston County Jail and arraigned in CAP court. The Livingston County District Attorney's Office recommended Summers be held on $5,000 cash bail or $15,000 bond. A judge instead remanded Summers to the custody of the sheriff on $1,500 cash bail or $3,000 bond, according to the sheriff's office.

https://news.postimees.ee/8558002/interv.text: Hungarian Foreign Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Anita Orbán told Postimees that abandoning Russian energy dependence will take more time. Photo: Hungarian MFA POSTIMEES NEWS INTERVIEW ⟩ Hungarian Foreign Minister: Changing the government is not enough Tarvo Madsen Ajakirjanik 4th October 2026, 17:33 Hungary needs more time to end its dependence on Russian energy. Hungary aims to meet the Maastricht criteria by the end of the term and adopt the euro. The process of unpacking the system built by Viktor Orbán is still ongoing. In a lengthy interview with Postimees, Hungarian Foreign Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Anita Orbán said that Hungary needs more time to free itself from Russian energy dependence. The dismantling of the system created by former Prime Minister Viktor Orbán is still underway, and it is not out of the question that the former prime minister could one day find himself in handcuffs. Postimees met with Anita Orbán on Thursday, October 1, in Budapest at the Hungarian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, shortly after her meeting with Estonian Foreign Minister Margus Tsahkna. It was also the first visit by an Estonian foreign minister to Hungary in the last seven years. The interview took place during a week when several major news stories had come out of Hungary: a couple of days earlier, two members of the previous government had been arrested, and some time before that, a number of Russian diplomats had been expelled from the country. Four months ago, most of Europe actually celebrated, and Estonia also celebrated what happened in Hungary. But is Hungary a totally different country now, for example, compared with what it was a year ago? I think, in that sense, yes. But I would like to say that the last few years were a deviation from the norm, and that was not the standard. So we are now pivoting back to our cultural heritage, to our heritage, to what we inherited – which is that our place is in Europe, in the heart of Europe, within the EU and NATO. And yes, even fellow compatriots who are coming back from abroad, or foreigners who are coming here, say that the mood, the air and everything are so different in Hungary now than they were a year ago. This is a country which is transitioning. This is a country which is going back to democracy, the rule of law, freedom of speech and freedom of the press. A lot has changed. And I think, if you look back a year, the hope was already there, but not many would have bet, I guess, that there would be such a transformative change. Péter Magyar, the man who overthrew Viktor Orbán. Four months ago, elections were held in Hungary, won by the TISZA party led by Magyar, after which the country, which had at times been seen as a pariah in Europe, took a new political direction. Credit: SOPA Images Limited/Alamy Live News Foto: SOPA Images Limited / Alamy Stock Photo But how much influence does Viktor Orbán still have in Hungary? I don't mean his personal political influence, but the whole system he created. How much of it is still left? A lot. Changing the government is not enough. You really need to unpack the system, and that's what you have been seeing since May. We have a pretty heavy legislative agenda, where we are really trying to undo all the state capture that took place under the previous government and reinstate the independence of all the institutions, from the Constitutional Court to various state authorities. We joined the European Public Prosecutor's Office as a clear sign of our commitment to zero tolerance for corruption. Just to give you an example, we created a new authority called the Asset Recovery and Protection Authority, whose task is to go after all the money that has been stolen, potentially recover it, and return it to public use. We abolished the Sovereignty Protection Office, which had been created and was harassing civil society and journalists. So we are doing a lot to change the system. And one more thing: it's not only about the institutions. His influence is also embedded in the economy and, unfortunately, to a certain extent, in people's mindset. Hungarian Foreign Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Anita Orbán. Foto: Ungari välisministeerium Anita Orbán Anita Orbán has been the Hungarian Foreign Minister and Deputy Prime Minister in Péter Magyar's government since May 2026. She joined the TISZA team before the spring elections, was at the top of the party's national electoral list, and was one of the most popular candidates. Before returning to politics, Orbán worked for years in the energy and telecommunications sectors. From 2010 to 2015, she was the Ambassador-at-Large for Energy Security in Viktor Orbán's government. She later worked for companies including Cheniere Energy, Tellurian, and Vodafone in London. Orbán studied economics, international relations, and diplomacy. She earned her PhD from The Fletcher School in 2007. A year later, her book "Power, Energy and the New Russian Imperialism" was published, which deals with Russia's use of energy resources as a tool of geopolitical influence. Despite sharing the same surname, Anita Orbán and Viktor Orbán are not related. You mentioned corruption as part of this. As I understand it, a couple of ministers from the Orbán era have already been detained. Yes. How far can this go? Could Viktor Orbán himself end up in handcuffs? We will see. We created this dedicated entity which I already mentioned, the National Asset Recovery and Protection Authority. We also have an independent prosecutor's office. What we committed to, and what we received the mandate for, is to go after all the stolen money. The population and society are asking that Hungary once again be a country where actions have consequences. So we really need to show and create new standards of integrity and politics. You have already seen the first example, so it is a very symbolic day and week for you to be here in Hungary. A lot has happened in the last couple of days, especially the fact that the first two former ministers were detained three days ago. Orbán-era ministers Miklós Seszták and Balázs Hankó were arrested at the end of September on suspicion of corruption. Seszták is suspected of taking bribes, Hankó of illegally distributing money from the National Cultural Fund. Both deny the charges. Pictured: Hankó's arrest. EPA/ROBERT HEGEDUS HUNGARY OUT Foto: Robert Hegedus Here in Estonia, we are currently struggling with a four percent budget deficit. As I understand it, yours is seven percent... More. ...but how do you deal with that without giving Fidesz a political weapon to use against you? First of all, we started from 8.3 percent. Then we took over the government, and it is now down to 7.5 percent thanks to the EU money we managed to recover. In addition, I think 91 percent of the budget that had been planned for this year had already been spent by the previous government by the end of April, so those were horrendous and enormous numbers. But, as you may have seen, in the first three months of this government we saved – I don't remember the number, but we will send it to you – quite a big chunk of money, and no austerity measures or anything like that were introduced. (More detailed information in the supplementary story accompanying the interview – ed.) No new burdens, just prudent spending. We cut unnecessary and luxury spending. We cut back on travel, on support for politicians, for example, and we are really mindful of how we spend public money. That created – and we will send you the figure – visible savings. Our goal is to meet the Maastricht criteria by the end of the term so that we can be eligible to introduce the euro. That means we will be very mindful of our public spending, but first we want to generate economic growth, and we are very, very mindful of how we spend. If I understand correctly, you hope to do this in a way that the impact on society is not too great, despite the difficult decisions. Is that possible? We shall see, and hopefully it is possible. We have a government off-site this weekend, and we will literally spend 48 hours discussing the budget, the economy and energy, and deciding on the main issues. I think the impact on society will also be a consequence of those decisions. Where did Hungary's money disappear? Viktor Orbán's government initially drafted the 2026 budget with the calculation that the deficit would remain at 3.7 percent of GDP. At the beginning of the year, the official forecast was raised to five percent, but by the time of the transfer of power, the Ministry of Finance's own documents were already calculating a 6.8 percent deficit. This number was not disclosed to the public. The picture turned out to be even worse. The new government, through a budget audit, found nearly 400 billion forints in additional costs that had not been accounted for in the previous budget. In addition, the Orbán government had included 969 billion forints from the European Union's recovery fund in this year's revenues, although the necessary steps to release the frozen funds had not been taken by then. According to the new government's assessment, if the previous policy had continued, the deficit would have reached 8.3 percent of GDP. Among the unbudgeted costs were 112 billion forints for settlements with the defense company N7, 72 billion to 4iG for space services, 56 billion for road construction, and 46 billion to cover a larger healthcare deficit. Pre-election spending also left its mark. By the end of April, the deficit of the central government budget was already 3.85 trillion forints, or 91.3 percent of the amount originally planned for the entire year. The Hungarian media has pointed to reasons including housing subsidies, special public sector payments, and the 13th and 14th month pensions. However, tightening spending does not mean the new government will abandon its new promises. This weekend, the cabinet will discuss the 2027 budget, which is supposed to include, among other things, a new pension package. The new government's first serious test will be whether it can reduce the budget deficit while simultaneously promising new benefits to society. According to the government's own data, in the first four months in office, it has managed to reduce this year's projected budget deficit from 8.3 percent to 7.5 percent of GDP. For years, Hungary was a country that Europe found it difficult to make decisions with. But what lesson did that give us? Is the current system in the European Union, where one country can block everything, sustainable, or should it be changed? I think there are a couple of decisions where you need consensus, and that is based on the EU treaties. There are also decisions where a qualified majority or just a majority is enough. So in that sense, I don't think this is about Hungary. This is about Europe as a whole: how we want Europe to work in foreign policy, security policy, as well as in most of its domestic agenda. I wouldn't add anything more for now. Viktor Orbán, who remains very politically active and promises to return to power soon, blocked numerous joint European Union decisions for years as prime minister. EPA/ROBERT HEGEDUS HUNGARY OUT Foto: Robert Hegedus There is a lot of talk in Europe about overall unity, but that is at the political level. In reality, member states always have different interests, for example when it comes to Russia and economic interests. But can you really achieve a common goal, for example with sanctions packages, if we keep excluding things and people, and someone is always fighting for themselves? I think we can. We have already accepted and approved the 21st sanctions package. Some would say they are not harsh enough. Listen, I think the strength of Europe is in unity. If you look at the history of Europe from the beginning until now and zoom out, it is remarkable what the European Union has achieved as an economy: in terms of freedom of movement, Schengen and borders, the customs union, as well as its own foreign and security policy. I think we have done well. Of course, you can always look at the glass as half full or half empty, but we have made great progress. The idea of the European Union is based on consensus decisions: you do not agree until you find the common denominator, and I think it is doable. Whether the sanctions package has an impact is a different story. We can debate whether it has had an impact, but we have also seen the sanctions packages being scaled up in Europe. I would dispute the idea that there is always someone standing in the way. Yes, we may see national interests which potentially prevent the kind of unity that the majority of member states would like to achieve. But this is exactly why the European Union is so powerful: it accommodates all the national interests into a common good. And look at it: how many countries want to join the European Union? It is a pretty powerful entity and has a strong attraction. Anita Orbán and Postimees journalist Tarvo Madsen in Budapest. Foto: Ungari välisministeerium If I understand correctly, Hungary has asked the United States to extend the exemption from sanctions on Russian oil and gas. How dependent is Hungary on Russia today? We are still buying a big chunk of our oil and natural gas supply from Russia, and we have a waiver which expires on November 21. Yes, we would like that waiver to be extended. Why so? Because what we inherited from the previous government is a pretty clear situation. Our economy, as well as residential heating and electricity, depend on that supply. So you just need more time to get rid of this dependence? We just need more time. In Estonia, we see Russia becoming more and more aggressive, especially through hybrid attacks. Has Russia also started to put more pressure on Hungary since the elections? Yes, we have seen what's happening in Estonia. We have also seen the attack against that defence company. Not only in Estonia, but across the Baltics and the Baltic Sea region. But no, we haven't seen any sabotage or attacks in Hungary since the election. But as I understand it, you just expelled ten Russian diplomats. Why? Because their activities were not in line with the Vienna Convention. You may not have read the news yet, but I can tell you that the Russian response arrived just today. Russia has also asked a few Hungarian diplomats to leave. According to Orbán, a number of Russian diplomats were expelled because they were not engaged in diplomacy in Budapest, but in something else. Foto: Ungari välisministeerium Russia is putting more and more pressure on Ukraine, especially on Kyiv. The situation in Kyiv is already near catastrophe. Can Europe help Ukraine get through this winter? Yes. We are most likely looking at a very tough winter for Ukraine, and what is really very sad is the increasing number of attacks which go beyond the front line and target infrastructure, key infrastructure, energy, as well as quite many civilians. There have been attacks on hospitals and, as far as I have seen, even schools. We are also very worried that it will be a very tough winter for Ukraine in terms of energy supply. Hungary is also giving quite substantial humanitarian aid to Ukraine. Now the EPF, the European Peace Facility, has also been unblocked. As you know, this is an instrument through which quite many European governments have supported Ukraine, and quite many governments have already pledged that whatever money is reimbursed to them for the support they have given will be allocated towards Ukraine. So I believe Ukraine will need a lot of support this winter, from humanitarian aid to potentially even equipment needed for heating or electricity generation. There are several elections coming up in Europe over the next few years. Could we see a point where Europe is no longer behind Ukraine? Of course, we see the positions of quite a few parties, and I think we have about eight elections coming up in Europe.

https://www.theguardian.com/commentisfre.text: ‘Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments.’ Photograph: José Luis Magaña/AP View image in fullscreen ‘Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments.’ Photograph: José Luis Magaña/AP Opinion Trump administration The Guardian view on Trump and Putin: Ukraine’s future is not theirs to bargain away Editorial Russia wants America and China to decide Ukraine’s future without Kyiv. Europe must challenge this dangerous return to diplomacy of the strong for the strong Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.25 EDT Last modified on Mon 19 Oct 2026 13.35 EDT Share D oes Vladimir Putin know exactly how to play Donald Trump? The history of chummy phone calls, high-profile meetings and attempts to bring Russia in from the cold certainly suggests that Moscow’s thuggish ruler has a hold on this American president. If Mr Trump agrees to negotiate Ukraine’s future with Mr Putin and China’s Xi Jinping without Ukraine at the table, he will have handed the Russian leader a victory before talks begin. The message will be that strongmen are ruling the world and determining the fate of weaker nations. Ukraine has the right to determine its future. That right cannot be waved away by a self-serving Russian proposal, however much it indulges Mr Trump’s belief that world affairs should be settled by powerful men. The scales are falling from European eyes. Trumpian America is raising doubts about whether it will help deter aggression or even honour its Nato commitments. If Washington now rewards Moscow and pressures Ukraine to accept a raw deal, it would be a betrayal . European governments would wonder where America might be in the future when their own security is threatened. View image in fullscreen Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping. Photograph: China Pool/Getty The Wall Street Journal laid out how Mr Putin is hoping to secure a diplomatic prize that dwarfs any US benefits. Mr Trump needs to bring down diesel prices before crucial midterm elections. So the Russian president has offered him a deal that helps the White House claim it is addressing such costs, despite most analysts saying that it won’t. In the same conversation, Mr Putin suggested a summit to end the war in Ukraine that would elevate Moscow and exclude Kyiv. China could also gain recognition as a diplomatic mediator, while Europe would be left out of discussions about ending a war on its continent. Reports suggest that the three leaders could meet at next month’s Asia-Pacific Economic Cooperation summit in China. American presidential power is meant to be constrained by law and democratic institutions. Mr Trump’s diesel deal appears to violate US law barring imports of Russian ‌energy until Moscow ends its aggression against Ukraine. More Republicans should find the courage to stand up to their bullying president. While doing so, they might also ask why the order to limit a satellite system used by Ukraine ​for battlefield communications and drone operations reportedly came from the White House . Heated denials from the US secretary of state, Marco Rubio , are no substitute for answers. A transatlantic breakdown in relations between European powers and the US is not inevitable. Mr Trump’s national security strategy last year called Europe “ strategically and culturally vital ”. But it also demanded that the continent take responsibility for its own defence. European governments must prepare to meet that challenge. History doesn’t repeat itself, but it often rhymes. Were Mr Trump to embrace Mr Putin’s trilateral summit, it would echo the Three Emperors’ League that brought together Germany, Austria-Hungary and Russia in 1873. Germany sought to isolate defeated France and contain Austro-Russian rivalry, while monarchies sought to defend themselves against revolution. The original arrangement quickly unravelled. Revived in 1881 , the league collapsed in 1887 as Vienna and Moscow failed to reconcile their Balkan ambitions. Agreement between powerful rulers provides no guarantee of a lasting settlement. Ukraine’s future cannot hang on bargains struck to stroke the egos of powerful men. Do you have an opinion on the issues raised in this article?
